name: Low-sodium for face de-puffing

lead: This practice means lowering salt intake to reduce water retention and facial puffiness, a common tip in looksmaxxing communities for a leaner, more defined face.

The chain is that sodium is involved in the osmotic regulation of water in body tissues, so less sodium means less retained water. Health guidance supports lower sodium for blood pressure, with the WHO recommending under 2,000 mg of sodium a day, about 5 g of salt. The sources reviewed do not discuss facial puffiness, and Wikipedia's acne article states evidence does not support a link between salt and acne.

paras: People cut processed and restaurant foods, season less, and read labels for sodium. Users report on morning facial puffiness within days to weeks.
Wikipedia notes the association between sodium intake and cardiovascular disease or mortality may be U-shaped, with risk at both high and low intakes.

web.title: Why you should watch your salt intake (Fox News)

angle.text: Users lower salt intake to reduce water retention and look slimmer and more defined in the face. Low sodium lowers blood pressure, and facial effects are not covered in the sources reviewed.

lead: Low-sodium for face de-puffing is the practice of reducing salt intake to lessen facial water retention. Followers aim for a leaner, more defined face, with sharper jawline and cheek contours and less puffiness under the eyes, especially in the morning.

The idea has a plausible basis in common medical descriptions. Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness lists excess dietary sodium among the causes of swelling around the eyes, along with sleep disruption, allergies, hormonal changes and ageing, and notes that puffiness is often worst after waking because fluid shifts while lying flat.[1] Dermatologist Marina Peredo of Mount Sinai was quoted in a 2017 Fox News piece saying that too much sodium can cause puffy under-eyes and facial bloating, and the article suggests potassium-rich foods and hydration.[2]

General sodium guidance addresses health rather than looks: the WHO recommends adults consume less than 2,000 mg of sodium a day, about 5 g of salt, and reducing sodium lowers blood pressure.[3] No controlled study measuring facial puffiness against sodium intake was identified.

paras: Developed countries generally recommend under 2,300 mg a day, and US guidance suggests 1,500 mg for some groups.[3] Reviews disagree on whether going below 2,300 mg is beneficial or harmful, and the link with cardiovascular outcomes has been described as U-shaped.[3]

Wikipedia lists allergies as the most common cause of eye swelling and describes ageing changes in which the skin around the eyes thins and the lower-lid fat pad enlarges, which it says is generally permanent. Raising the head while sleeping and cold compresses are described as options for fluid-related puffiness, and persistent swelling can signal a medical condition.[1] These factors mean sodium is one of several contributors that people discuss.
No studies found on dietary sodium and facial puffiness. Studies of sodium reduction concern blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes.[3]
